paragraphs: The son of Rabbi Yishmael’s sister.

In the Babylonian Talmud he is mentioned only as Ben Dama, but in the Jerusalem Talmud he is mentioned as Rabbi Elazar ben Dama. Hyman places him among the leading sages of the generation already in the days of his uncle Rabbi Yishmael, as in Menachot 99b: Ben Dama, the son of Rabbi Yishmael’s sister, asked Rabbi Yishmael: “Someone like me, who has learned the whole Torah — may he learn Greek wisdom?” and he did not permit him. In Tosefta Shevuot, chapter 3, he asked Rabbi Yishmael about a law of testimony, and he called him “Ben Dama, my son.” In Berakhot 56b he asked Rabbi Yishmael: “I saw in my dream that my two cheeks fell off.” He said to him: “Two Roman troops plotted evil against you and died.” The cause of his death is related in Avodah Zarah 27b: an incident with Ben Dama (in the Jerusalem Talmud, end of Shabbat, chapter 14, and Avodah Zarah, chapter 2, end of halakhah 2, it reads Rabbi Elazar ben Dama), the son of Rabbi Yishmael’s sister, whom a snake bit. Yaakov of Kefar Sekhanya (in the Jerusalem Talmud there, of Kefar Sana, in the name of Yeshu ben Pandera) came to heal him, and Rabbi Yishmael did not let him. He said to him: “Yishmael my brother, let him, and I will bring a verse from the Torah that it is permitted.” He did not manage to finish the matter before his soul departed and he died. Rabbi Yishmael applied to him: “Fortunate are you, Ben Dama, for your body is pure and your soul departed in purity, and you did not transgress the words of your colleagues.”

In the book Heikhalot Rabbati, chapter 4, [it says] that Rabbi Elazar ben Dama was one of those executed by the government; Hyman considers this a scribal error and proposes Rabbi Yehudah ben Dama; see his entry.

notes.text: ולא התירו is singular, Yishmael did not permit him. The supplied כפר סנא is rendered KefarSana; Sama was an unsupported draft normalization. Yeshuב״פ is rendered benPandera as disclosed in the original note. Saved Davidson Berakhot56b retains the dream’s cheeks; AZ27b supports BenDama speaking to Yishmael and the unfinished proposed proof. Hyman’s Heikhalot name emendation stays conjectural.

The directly consulted Avodah Zarah 27b preserves Ben Dama addressing Yishmael, the refused healing and the unfinished proposed proof. The following eulogy also has material omitted by Hyman, which is not inserted into his abridgment. The Greek-wisdom permission remains singular; Kefar Sana, Yeshu ben Pandera and the dream’s cheeks remain as disclosed in the current note. Hyman’s leading-generation and only-name assertions and Heikhalot emendation are not independently proved by this one locus.
